figures.alt: Diagram showing haemoglobin in red blood cells carrying oxygen and carbon dioxide. Carbon monoxide binds tightly, preventing oxygen transport.

specPoints.text: know that a fuel is a substance that, when burned, releases heat energy
know the possible products of complete and incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons with oxygen in the air
understand why carbon monoxide is poisonous, in terms of its effect on the capacity of blood to transport oxygen references to haemoglobin are not required

primer.text: From Crude Oil you already know where fuels come from and which engines burn them. This note follows the burning itself: what a fuel is, the products when oxygen is plentiful or scarce, and the quiet danger carbon monoxide poses to the blood that carries oxygen.

lessons.title: Fuels and complete combustion
lessons.opening: A fuel is any substance that gives out heat when it burns, and fossil fuels power most of modern life. This lesson defines fuels, lists the fossil ones, and writes the complete-burning equation for propane.
keyPoints: A fuel is a substance that releases heat energy when it burns, an exothermic change.
The fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas, with oil shales and tar sands also listed, all finite.
Petrol fuels cars, kerosene fuels aircraft, diesel fuels heavy vehicles, and coal runs power stations.
Natural gas consists mainly of methane, and all fossil fuels contain carbon, hydrogen and some sulfur.
With excess oxygen, hydrocarbons burn completely: C3H8 + 5O2 gives 3CO2 + 4H2O.

low.restatement: A fuel gives out heat as it burns. Burn a hydrocarbon with plenty of oxygen and the only products are carbon dioxide and water. Both products are oxides, fully combined with the oxygen supplied by the air.
low.analogy: A well-fed fire is a tidy accountant: every carbon atom leaves as carbon dioxide and every hydrogen leaves as water, with nothing left unaccounted.
low.examPointer: Define a fuel through heat released on burning, then attach the excess-oxygen condition to the products list.

medium.restatement: Fuels release heat energy on burning because burning is exothermic, and the fossil fuels from crude oil include coal, oil and natural gas. In excess oxygen a hydrocarbon burns completely, so propane yields carbon dioxide and water in the ratio its formula dictates: three CO2 and four H2O per molecule.
medium.analogy: Complete burning is a full-refund exchange: the oxygen-rich shop takes every carbon and hydrogen and returns them as their fully oxidised products, nothing partial, nothing owed.
medium.examPointer: Predict products from the fuel formula and the oxygen supply, and balance the equation before quoting it in an answer.

check.stem: What is the definition of a fuel?

options.text: A substance that releases heat energy when it burns
options.explanation: Heat output on burning is the whole definition, with burning itself exothermic.

options.text: Any liquid that can be poured into an engine
options.explanation: Solid coal is a fuel too; physical state is not part of the definition.

options.text: A substance that absorbs heat as it reacts
options.explanation: Fuels give heat out; absorbing heat is the endothermic opposite.

options.text: Any substance containing carbon
options.explanation: Carbon content alone does not make a fuel; the heat release on burning does.

check.stem: Which list contains only fossil fuels?

options.text: Coal, oil and natural gas
options.explanation: These three head the fossil fuel list, joined by oil shales and tar sands.

options.text: Coal, ethanol and natural gas
options.explanation: Ethanol is not a fossil fuel on this list; it belongs to the alcohols family.

options.text: Wood, oil and bitumen
options.explanation: Wood is not a fossil fuel; it is recent plant material.

options.text: Peat, hydrogen and oil
options.explanation: Hydrogen is not fossil; the fossil set is coal, oil, gas, shales and tar sands.

check.stem: What are the products of the complete combustion of propane, C3H8?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: Excess oxygen turns all three carbons into CO2 and all eight hydrogens into water.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.explanation: CO appears only when oxygen is limited; complete burning goes all the way to CO2.

options.text: Carbon and steam only
options.explanation: Plain carbon is the soot of incomplete burning, not the complete case.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide and water
options.explanation: Propane itself carries no sulfur; SO2 comes from impurities in other fuels.
Three carbon atoms in propane must all appear as three CO2 molecules on the right.
One CO2 would strand two of the three carbons from propane.
Five belongs to the oxygen coefficient; the carbon count fixes the CO2 at three.
Eight counts hydrogens, not carbon dioxide molecules.

check.stem: Why do fossil fuels all contain small quantities of sulfur?

options.text: Because sulfur impurities are present in the fuel sources themselves
options.explanation: The crude and coal carry traces of sulfur from their formation, which survives into the refined fuel.

options.text: Because sulfur is added deliberately during refining
options.explanation: Nothing is added; the sulfur is an unwanted leftover from the source material.

options.text: Because engines manufacture sulfur during use
options.explanation: Engines only release what the fuel already contains.

options.text: Because sulfur dissolves out of the air into the fuel
options.explanation: The sulfur comes with the fuel from the ground, not from the air afterwards.

lessons.title: Incomplete combustion
lessons.opening: When oxygen runs short, the same hydrocarbons burn messily and dangerously. This lesson follows the fuel into boilers, stoves and engines where oxygen is scarce, and tracks the carbon into monoxide and soot.
keyPoints: Incomplete combustion happens when there is insufficient oxygen to burn the fuel fully.
It occurs in appliances such as boilers and stoves, and inside internal combustion engines.
The products are unburnt fuel as soot, carbon monoxide and water.
In even poorer oxygen supply, methane gives carbon soot: CH4 + O2 -> C + 2H2O.

low.restatement: Shortage of oxygen stops the carbon reaching dioxide. It leaves the flame as carbon monoxide or as black soot, while the hydrogen still escapes as water. Boilers, stoves and car engines are the everyday places where this shortage happens.
low.analogy: It is a queue at a door that is too narrow: only some carbons get the full oxygen service, and the rest leave half-served or not served at all.
low.examPointer: Name soot, carbon monoxide and water together when asked for incomplete products, and tie them to limited oxygen.

medium.restatement: In insufficient oxygen the hydrocarbon burns incompletely: the hydrogen still forms water, but carbon emerges as carbon monoxide or as soot of unburnt fuel. The two methane equations show the ladder, from 2CO with moderate shortage down to plain carbon when oxygen is scarcest, and boilers, stoves and engines are the everyday stages for it.
medium.analogy: Think of oxygen as budget: with a cut budget the carbon buys the cheap monoxide ticket, and with the budget almost gone it cannot travel at all and stays as soot.
medium.examPointer: Predict which carbon product forms by judging how severe the oxygen shortage is, and quote the matching balanced equation.

check.stem: Which condition causes incomplete combustion in a boiler?

options.text: Insufficient oxygen reaching the flame
options.explanation: Starved flames cannot fully oxidise the carbon, so CO and soot appear.

options.text: Excess oxygen reaching the flame
options.explanation: Excess oxygen drives the complete reaction to CO2 and water instead.

options.text: The presence of water vapour in the air
options.explanation: Water vapour is a product of burning, not a cause of incomplete burning.

options.text: Using methane instead of propane
options.explanation: Any hydrocarbon burns incompletely if oxygen is short; the fuel choice is not the cause.

check.stem: In the equation 2CH4 + 3O2 -> 2CO + 4H2O, why does only 3O2 appear instead of 4O2?

options.text: Because the limited oxygen cannot fully oxidise the carbon to dioxide
options.explanation: Three O2 is all the supply allows, so carbon stops at monoxide and the equation reflects the shortage.

options.text: Because methane contains less carbon when oxygen is scarce
options.explanation: The methane formula never changes; only the oxygen supply changes.

options.text: Because water needs no oxygen at all
options.explanation: Every water molecule carries an oxygen atom, which is part of the same budget.

options.text: Because the 3 balances the equation more neatly
options.explanation: Coefficients follow atom counts, not tidiness; the 3 records the real oxygen limit.

check.stem: What is soot, in the language of this note?

options.text: Unburnt fuel appearing as carbon particles
options.explanation: Soot is the carbon that never found enough oxygen to leave as an oxide.

options.text: Ash from the minerals in the fuel
options.explanation: The note names soot as unburnt hydrocarbon, not mineral ash.

options.text: Another name for water vapour
options.explanation: Water is a separate, fully oxidised product; soot is carbon.

options.text: The catalyst used inside engines
options.explanation: Catalysts are separate hardware; soot is a combustion product.

check.stem: Methane burns with equation CH4 + O2 -> C + 2H2O. What does this show about the oxygen supply?

options.text: The supply is so poor that carbon cannot oxidise at all
options.explanation: Carbon emerges as the bare element, the bottom rung of the incomplete ladder.

options.text: The supply is generous, so burning is complete
options.explanation: Complete burning would show CO2, not bare carbon, on the right.

options.text: The supply is irrelevant to this equation
options.explanation: The one-oxygen supply is exactly what forces the carbon product down to C.

options.text: The methane has decomposed without burning
options.explanation: The reaction still burns the hydrogen to water; it is incomplete burning, not mere breakdown.

check.stem: Why does incomplete combustion matter beyond the equation?

options.text: Because carbon monoxide formed this way is poisonous to people
options.explanation: The next section shows CO binding in the blood; the equation is where the danger starts.

options.text: Because soot makes the water products acidic
options.explanation: Soot is carbon; the acid-rain story belongs to sulfur and nitrogen oxides.

options.text: Because incomplete burning releases no energy
options.explanation: Heat is still released, just less efficiently than complete burning.

options.text: Because boilers stop working entirely
options.explanation: Appliances keep running; the hazard is the gas released, not a shutdown.

lessons.title: Why carbon monoxide is poisonous
sourceHeadings: How carbon monoxide affects the body
lessons.opening: Carbon monoxide is invisible, odourless and tasteless, which makes it a silent hazard. This lesson explains how inhaled CO steals the blood oxygen-carrying capacity that tissues depend on.
keyPoints: Carbon monoxide is a highly poisonous gas from incomplete burning of carbon-containing fuels.
It is odourless, colourless and tasteless, so it can be inhaled without being noticed.
Inhaled CO is absorbed into red blood cells and binds tightly to the molecules that normally carry oxygen.
This binding cuts the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen round the body.
Haemoglobin binds CO around 200 to 250 times more strongly than oxygen, forming stable carboxyhaemoglobin.

low.restatement: Breathed in, carbon monoxide hops into red blood cells and grips the oxygen-carrying molecules tightly. The blood then carries less oxygen, so tissues go short. The victim never smells or tastes anything wrong.
low.analogy: CO is a squatter with the strongest grip in the building: it occupies the seats meant for oxygen and refuses to leave, so fewer oxygen passengers get a ride.
low.examPointer: The key marking point is reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood; the exam hint confirms haemoglobin detail is optional.

medium.restatement: Inhaled carbon monoxide passes from the lungs into red blood cells and binds to the oxygen-transport molecules there. Because haemoglobin grips CO about 200 to 250 times more strongly than oxygen, the binding is preferential and effectively irreversible, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and cutting the capacity of blood to transport oxygen to tissues.
medium.analogy: Picture a taxi rank where one passenger monopolises every cab two hundred times more firmly than the real customers: the fleet keeps driving, but almost nobody who needs a ride gets one.
medium.examPointer: If you use haemoglobin, state both halves: CO binds irreversibly, and less oxygen is carried round the body.

check.stem: Why is carbon monoxide especially dangerous in the home?

options.text: It is odourless, colourless and tasteless, so it goes unnoticed
options.explanation: With no sensory warning, a person can inhale it without realising anything is present.

options.text: It has a strong smell that people ignore
options.explanation: The danger is the absence of smell, not the ignoring of one.

options.text: It stains walls green as a warning
options.explanation: CO is colourless and leaves no visible trace to warn anyone.

options.text: It explodes on contact with air
options.explanation: The hazard is poisoning through inhalation, not explosion.

check.stem: According to the specification, what is the key point about carbon monoxide poisoning?

options.text: It reduces the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen
options.explanation: The exam hint names exactly this as the marking point examiners look for.

options.text: It dissolves the walls of the lungs
options.explanation: The mechanism is oxygen transport, not physical damage to lung tissue.

options.text: It thickens the blood until it cannot flow
options.explanation: Flow thickness is not the claim; carrying capacity is.

options.text: It prevents red blood cells from being made
options.explanation: Existing cells are hijacked; production of new cells is not part of the story.

check.stem: How much more strongly does haemoglobin bind carbon monoxide than oxygen?

options.text: Around 200 to 250 times more strongly
options.explanation: The detailed explanation quotes that range as the affinity gap.

options.text: About the same strength
options.explanation: If the strengths matched, CO would be far less dangerous than it is.

options.text: About half as strongly
options.explanation: CO binds far more strongly than oxygen, not more weakly.

options.text: Around 2 to 5 times more strongly
options.explanation: The gap is two orders of magnitude larger, which is why CO wins so completely.

check.stem: What name is given to the stable compound formed when haemoglobin binds CO?

options.text: Carboxyhaemoglobin
options.explanation: The detailed explanation names carboxyhaemoglobin as the stable product of the binding.

options.text: Oxyhaemoglobin
options.explanation: That is the oxygen-carrying form CO prevents from forming.

options.text: Carboxylic acid
options.explanation: That is an organic acid family, unrelated to the blood compound here.

options.text: Carbonic acid
options.explanation: Carbonic acid belongs to CO2 in water, a different gas and a different story.

check.stem: Is referring to haemoglobin required in your exam answer?

options.text: No, but recent mark schemes accept it if the oxygen-transport point is stated
options.explanation: The spec excludes the requirement, yet mark schemes allow the detail alongside the key point.

options.text: Yes, the full haemoglobin mechanism must be quoted
options.explanation: The specification explicitly says references to haemoglobin are not required.

options.text: No, and mentioning haemoglobin loses the mark
options.explanation: Mark schemes accept it; only the key point must not be omitted.

options.text: Only for extended writing questions
options.explanation: The rule does not switch with question type; the key point is always the target.

glossary.definition: A substance that releases heat energy when it burns, in an exothermic reaction.
Burning in excess oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water.
Burning in insufficient oxygen, producing carbon monoxide or soot as well as water.
A colourless, odourless, tasteless and highly poisonous gas made when fuels burn in poor oxygen supply.
The molecule in red blood cells that binds oxygen; carbon monoxide binds it far more strongly, blocking oxygen transport.

workedExample.prompt: a) Define a fuel and write the equation for the complete combustion of propane. b) Write the equations for the incomplete combustion of methane, for the carbon monoxide and soot cases. c) Explain why carbon monoxide is poisonous.
steps: a) A fuel is a substance that, when burned, releases heat energy (an exothermic reaction); in excess oxygen propane burns completely: C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O.
b) With insufficient oxygen (in boilers, stoves and engines): 2CH4 + 3O2 → 2CO + 4H2O gives carbon monoxide, and in an even poorer supply CH4 + O2 → C + 2H2O gives carbon soot.
c) Inhaled carbon monoxide binds to the oxygen-carrying molecules in red blood cells, reducing the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen around the body.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Fuel = releases heat on burning; C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. b) 2CH4 + 3O2 → 2CO + 4H2O; CH4 + O2 → C + 2H2O. c) CO binds in the blood, cutting its oxygen-carrying capacity.
